P01.note: The warships sentence (anchored across the harbor mouth, turned back every freighter) states the blockade outright. 'Annexed' dies on the island's flag and clerks staying, 'boycotted' on the alliance turning back its own buyers' ships; 'bombarded' has no planted kill but nothing in the passage describes firing, so it is weak.

P02.note: 'All twenty-eight of its crew, whose bodies were never recovered' with battened hatches hands over 'tomb', and 'true tomb' for a wreck is a stock phrase. 'Trellis' is off-topic for a steel hull on a surface read (and 'bare of growth' kills it), 'strongbox' dies on 'only ballast', 'tripwire' on the ferries passing safely over ninety feet of water.

P03.note: 'Crated' fails on a surface read: stones 'broken into rubble' were not packed for moving. 'Condemned' is the real near-miss and dies only on 'walls sound and its tower true', but a council can condemn a building for clearance regardless of soundness, so it stays close; 'commandeered' dies on the site becoming a parking lot rather than being taken into use.

P04.note: 'Pirated' is a good lure from 'cheap editions appeared in every city' and dies only on the printer's license and her share arriving; 'plagiarized' dies on the actress naming the poet each night, 'panned' on the papers naming poems among the season's best, and panned/popularized is an opposite pair.

P05.note: Requires combining the wall's riverbank footing below the waterline with the river rising nearly to its top and flooding the meadows on either side. 'Hearth' (fruit-wall warmth) dies on frost blackening trees beside the wall too, 'firebreak' on the fire dying in the pasture on the open north side, 'fence' on the north side lying open.

P06.note: The treasury buying a controlling share of all four papers decides 'nationalized' in one sentence. 'Muzzled' is the wartime cliché and dies on 'No official read those pages' plus the papers attacking ministers; 'mobilized' dies on refusing the recruiting notices; 'impoverished' on the pages doubling with treasury money.

P07.note: 'Incised' rests on the slot cut by the river beneath the glacier, attributing the meltwater's cut to the glacier. 'Mantled' is killed in its till sense by all rock lying in one ridge at the mouth, but in its plain sense (covered, blanketed) it literally describes a half-mile glacier lying frozen over a valley whose soil survived beneath it, so it remains defensible; 'milled' dies on the soil surviving, 'littered' on the single ridge.

P08.note: Good item: 'kidney' is the textbook marsh metaphor and dies on the nitrate leaving at creek levels, 'net' on the water running just as brown, 'lung' on oxygen matching the bay; 'kitchen' needs the rotting grass drift plus the shrimp guts packed with it.

P09.note: Key needs the swells breaking along the bar combined with boats at the piers riding out storms. 'Turnstile' dies on ships crossing several abreast on every tide, 'tollbooth' on unpiloted passage by public buoys, 'wharf' on ships tying up at the town's piers rather than at the bar.

P10.note: 'Roadmap' is off-topic on a surface read; nothing in a barley list is about routes. 'Recipe' dies on each line giving a day, 'payroll' on the barley being what one farmer brought in; the storehouse keeper's seal and the farmhouse jar then settle 'receipt'.

P11.note: 'Lifted' fails on a surface read: nothing about sand raises a village (and the doorways open at their original height). 'Nibbled' is the real lure and dies on the families keeping every house and garden; 'lashed' dies on the 'still hollow'; buried roads and a three-day walk give 'imprisoned'.

P12.note: 'The soil holds twice the nitrogen' hands over 'fertilized' in one sentence. 'Denuded' (the grazing cliché) dies on grass growing taller and greener, 'groomed' on uneven tussocks, 'furrowed' on no worn paths; each distractor is matched to its own negating phrase.

P13.note: 'Reduced' is lured by half as many meadow elk and dies on the valley total barely changing; 'rattled' (landscape of fear) dies on elk grazing heads down as long as before; 'rejuvenated' on the herd growing older. Key needs the meadow-to-timber shift combined with the stable total.

P14.note: 'Bridge' rests on the clams descending from two spring fields on opposite sides and young reaching a third. But the passage plants 'a seafloor where food is otherwise scarce' and scavengers stripping a forty-ton carcass, so 'banquet' literally describes what it reports and nothing in the text kills it; only 'cupboard' dies cleanly (bones bare within two years).

P15.note: The earthquake sentence (stripe stepping sideways, asphalt broken across both lanes) decides 'ruptured' alone. 'Rutted' and 'rippled' die on trucks leaving the asphalt level, 'raised' on stakes showing the roadbed at its laid height.

P16.note: The kneeling at a spring that 'a parish legend said had cured a blind shepherd', drinking in turn and tying cloth strips is a textbook holy-well pilgrimage; one sentence hands it over. 'Raid' and 'roundup' have nothing in the passage about them beyond the ponies left grazing, and 'pageant' has no audience.

P17.note: 'Corridor' is the strong lure (strip between two forests) and dies on no vole moving over half a mile and stretch-local gene variants; 'cemetery' dies on strip voles living as long. 'Cafeteria' is weak: nothing in the passage is about food. The key 'cage' is acceptable but harsher than the evidence (voles simply stay), so the item is won by elimination.

P18.note: 'Twice as wide and twice as tall', the harbor going from one inch to two and the scale bar doubling state 'enlarged' outright. Each distractor is struck by one planted phrase: 'flipped' by north at the top of both, 'doctored' by every feature where the survey puts it, 'gilded' by the sea bare of ornament.

P19.note: Guidebooks telling drovers to walk toward the tongue that points at the road notch decides 'signpost' in one sentence. 'Timepiece' dies on the river barely changing between morning and night, 'thermometer' on the front holding one ledge through warm and cold, 'storeroom' on meltwater sinking and the river running low in dry summers.

P20.note: Evenings by the fire reading newspapers and playing cards give 'parlor'. 'Pawnshop' dies on miners paying cash for tobacco and nothing more, 'repository' on the safe holding only his own takings, 'pharmacy' on the bottles holding whiskey.

P21.note: The sandbar coming to rest over the wreck and the hull found only by probing give 'entombed'. 'Gnawed' dies on the deck sound enough to hold a nail, 'encrusted' on 'smooth and pale', 'dismantled' on an intact hull with full casks.

P22.note: 'Mined' fails on a surface read: nothing removed anything from the wreck. 'Interred' dies on bare rock; 'mummified' is lured by timbers 'hard and sound' (a literal fit for preservation) but the ship was rolled apart and strewn; 'jostled' fits the storms rolling it, though it is mild for a ship broken apart over a quarter mile.

P23.note: Good item: 'naturalized' dies on keeping the names, fjord and money; 'mutilated' on every chapter kept; 'lightened' on every drowning and hunger told in full; 'manicured' needs the broken-to-balanced style change plus the reviewers' 'grace'.

P24.note: 'Heeled until the sea poured over their rails and did not come back up' and 'upturned hulls' define capsizing. Each distractor has one planted kill: 'becalmed' by the squall, 'beached' by 'miles from any shore', 'blinded' by 'in plain sight of them'.

P25.note: 'Depository' is the strong lure (cool dry salt mines really do store art, and the paintings were held there) and dies only on each painting returning within a year or two repaired; 'gallery' dies on 'closed to the public', 'dump' on the paintings going back up; restorers cleaning and patching give 'hospital'.

P26.note: 'The surface barely carried a leaf' hands over 'stilled'. 'Soured' dies on trout feeding as above, 'walled' on cattle grazing to reedy edges, 'siphoned' on the whole stream spilling over the wheel.

P27.note: 'Stones there rocked at a touch, and a dozen lay in the grass' hands over 'dislodged', and dislodged/fortified is an opposite pair so 'fortified' is struck as one end of it. 'Dried' dies on matching moisture readings, 'etched' on clean stone faces.

P28.note: 'Chilled' (the deep-release cliché) dies on the release drawn from just beneath the sunlit surface and bass spawning below; 'clogged' on spring floods scouring the gravel bars; 'churned' on the steady release; 'bled' needs the canal taking two thirds plus the river a third as wide.

P29.note: 'Sapped' requires combining no deaths in the drought, a decade of narrow rings and beetle deaths a healthy pine would resist. 'Winnowed' literally fits one tree in five being removed and dies only on 'large and small alike' plus the deaths coming later; 'toppled' dies on the dead staying standing, 'scorched' on green needles.

P30.note: The last sentence (less nitrogen in the topsoil, more in the well) decides 'leached' alone, with water sinking through loose sand. 'Manured' dies on clear water and less nitrogen, 'mired' on the corn going in on schedule; 'mulched' has no planted kill and nothing in the passage is about a surface layer.

P31.note: 'Sorted' (the fluvial cliché) dies on the same size mix at cliffs and sea, 'stacked' on stones lying wherever they stopped, 'sanded' on broken pebbles still fitting edge to edge; 'stained' needs the orange-outside, gray-inside stones below the spring plus the orange film.

P32.note: 'Mixer' needs both groups arriving on the same evenings plus cross-group friendships rising. 'Magnet' literally fits nearly all visitors walking in and staying two hours and dies only because it says nothing of the mixing; 'muffler' dies on lawns sloping open to the highway, 'junction' on visitors staying rather than passing through.

P33.note: Standardized spelling and added sentence breaks give 'tidied'. 'Tightened' dies on every notebook sentence being in the book, 'spliced' on 'in the same order', 'softened' on the curses appearing in full; each distractor is paired with one negating sentence.

P34.note: Arriving at dusk, wrapping in mucus and lying still until dawn give 'bedroom'. 'Canteen' dies on algae growing a foot long (ungrazed), 'ballroom' on 'lie still'; 'clinic' (cleaning-station lure) dies only indirectly, since the fish protect themselves from parasites rather than being treated.

P35.note: 'Patrolled' (the ant-plant textbook answer) dies on caterpillars chewing both kinds alike, 'propagated' on seeds dropping beneath the parent, 'parasitized' on banded shrubs growing just as tall; 'pollinated' needs flowers swelling into pods only where an ant crawled through.

P36.note: Running a mile or more before nearly every kill gives 'chased'. 'Ambushed' dies on that same run, 'cowed' on elk browsing the willows as low as ever, 'corralled' on the herd ranging over the whole valley floor.

P37.note: Workers carrying aphids in their jaws to the youngest leaves decides 'herded'. 'Devoured' dies on numbers rising all summer, 'drugged' on aphids walking as quickly on crossed leaves; 'garnered' has no planted kill but gathering aphids as a harvest is not what the passage describes.

P38.note: 'Ransacked' literally fits soldiers clearing half the galleries in a night and leaving empty frames, and dies only on the numbered crates signed for by the towns on the labels; 'requisitioned' dies on the pieces going to those towns, 'ransomed' on no payment asked; 'repatriated' needs the century-old seizure plus the return to the labeled towns.

P39.note: The final sentence 'the meadow along the creek stays green while the valley next door turns brown' echoes the key word 'greened' directly. Each distractor has one planted kill: 'flooded' by 'under no standing water', 'dredged' by silt raising the pond floors, 'deforested' by aspens as thick as next door.

P40.note: The duke's deeds and treasury chests behind two iron doors decide 'vault' in one sentence. 'Tavern' dies on travelers buying wine at the village inn, 'sanatorium' on the sick being turned away, 'scriptorium' on 'none was ever copied'.

tells: One-kill-per-distractor template: in most items each wrong option is paired with exactly one planted negating phrase (often in sentences after the blank), so a solver can match options to their denials and take the one left unnegated without understanding the passage's logic: P05, P06, P08, P09, P12, P13, P15, P18, P19, P20, P21, P23, P24, P26, P27, P28, P29, P31, P33, P35, P36, P39, P40.

The cliché / textbook word for the topic is usually a distractor (killed by one planted fact) rather than the key: kidney P08, corridor P17, sorted P31, denuded P12, reduced P13, muzzled P06, pirated P04, chilled P28, patrolled P35, nibbled P11, depository P25, condemned P03. Exceptions where the cliché is keyed (tomb P02, pilgrimage P16, greened P39) are the easy items.

Paired worlds reuse one frame with contrasting keys: P21/P22 (merchant ship with iron bars and wine, divers in 1990; sand burial vs rock tumbling) and P13/P36 (wolves return to an elk valley; in both the fear word, rattled/cowed, is a distractor and the plain behavioural word is keyed).

'[Observer] calls/describes X as the [place]'s ______' noun-metaphor template recurs: P05, P08, P09, P10, P14, P17, P19, P20, P25, P32, P34, P40; and 'the [report] concludes/says that [agent] had ______ the [thing]' recurs across P07, P12, P22, P23, P26, P27, P29, P30, P33, P37, P39.
Alliterative option sets (P03 c-, P04 p-, P13 r-, P15 r-, P28 c-, P30 m-, P35 p-, P38 r-) are a repeated template, though I found no letter or sound that predicts the key within them.
